body:
**Charlie Munger**
- **Mental models (said).** Munger argues for a "latticework of mental models" drawn from several disciplines. He also says: "Over the long term, it's hard for a stock to earn a much better return than the business which underlies it earns. If the business earns 6% on capital over 40 years and you hold it for that 40 years, you're not going to make much different than a 6% return—even if you originally buy it at a huge discount. Conversely, if a business earns 18% on capital over 20 or 30 years, even if you pay an expensive looking price, you'll end up with one hell of a result." — "A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom," USC Business School, 1994 (transcript widely reproduced, e.g. [Farnam Street](https://fs.blog/great-talks/a-lesson-on-worldly-wisdom/)) [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Inversion (said).** "Invert, always invert" (borrowed from the mathematician Jacobi). In practice you ask what would make the investment fail and then avoid those conditions. The bias catalogue is in "The Psychology of Human Misjudgment" (1995). [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Munger's influence on Smith (commentary).** Fundsmith's approach has been described as "the Charlie Munger approach." — [GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/768842/fundsmith-the-charlie-munger-approach)

**Buffett's results as factor exposure (academic, see section 4)**
- Berkshire's Sharpe ratio was 0.79. Its alpha "becomes insignificant when controlling for exposures to Betting-Against-Beta and Quality-Minus-Junk factors." The authors conclude that Buffett's returns are a "reward for leveraging cheap, safe, quality stocks," with average leverage of about 1.7:1. — [Frazzini, Kabiller & Pedersen, "Buffett's Alpha," NBER w19681](https://www.nber.org/papers/w19681.pdf); [FAJ 2018](https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/en/research/financial-analysts-journal/2018/faj-v74-n4-3)

**Benjamin Graham**
- **Margin of safety (said).** "Margin of Safety" is the central concept of investment, set out in chapter 20 of *The Intelligent Investor*. [primary, not re-fetched]
- **Defensive investor criteria (said, ch. 14 of *The Intelligent Investor*, revised ed.).** [primary, not re-fetched]
  - adequate size
  - strong financial condition: current ratio ≥ 2, and long-term debt no greater than net current assets
  - earnings stability: positive earnings in each of the past 10 years
  - uninterrupted dividends for 20 years
  - EPS growth of at least one-third over 10 years, using 3-year averages at each end
  - P/E ≤ 15 on 3-year average earnings
  - P/B ≤ 1.5, or P/E × P/B ≤ 22.5
- **The Graham Number.** It is √(22.5 × EPS × BVPS), derived from the last criterion above.

body:
- Avoiding ruin: Buffett on LTCM ("risked what they did have and did need"). — [Novel Investor](https://novelinvestor.com/buffetts-lessons-long-term-capital-management/). Buffett also says you don't need a 160 IQ: temperament matters more than intellect. — [Value Research](https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/225179/buffett-right-dont-need-160-iq-good-investor/)
- Patience and time: Housel's Buffett analysis, in Section 5. — [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/05/03/most-of-warren-buffetts-wealth-came-after-age-65-heres-why.html)
- Owner or founder route: Kaplan & Rauh (69% started businesses) and Bessembinder's concentration finding, in Section 1.
- Research predictors of retail success:
  - low turnover and low costs ([Barber & Odean](https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/odean/Papers%20current%20versions/Individual_Investor_Performance_Final.pdf))
  - less disposition effect and higher IQ ([Grinblatt et al.](https://conference.nber.org/confer/2009/BEF09/Grinblatt_Keloharju_Linnainmaa.pdf))
  - less volatile, allocation-style vehicles with smaller behavior gaps ([Morningstar](https://www.morningstar.com/business/insights/research/mind-the-gap-2025))
  - in India, larger equity holdings and more experience link to lower F&O loss rates ([SEBI FY26 via CorpLaw](https://www.corplawupdates.in/updates/sebi-equity-derivatives-retail-trader-study-fy26))
- Mauboussin: in luck-heavy activities, focus on *process* over outcomes, and judge by long samples. — [Advisor Perspectives](https://www.advisorperspectives.com/articles/2012/12/11/luck-versus-skill-in-investing-new-insights-from-the-world-of-sports-and-beyond)

body:
`case_study:satyam-2009` | 2009-01-07 | tickers: US-SAY | confidence: verified

On 7 Jan 2009 chairman B. Ramalinga Raju confessed that Rs 5,040 cr of the Rs 5,361 cr cash and bank balance at Sep-2008 did not exist (total manipulation ~Rs 7,000 cr incl. fake interest accrual, understated liabilities, overstated debtors). Stock: 52-week high ~Rs 544 (2008) -> Rs 179 (6 Jan 2009) -> Rs 39.95 close on 7 Jan (-78%) -> ~Rs 6-7 intraday within days; Tech Mahindra bought control in Apr 2009 at Rs 58/share. Visible-in-advance flags: (1) a huge cash pile earning low interest (other income far below what Rs 5,000 cr+ should yield) while the company did not pay large dividends or buy back stock; (2) debtor days above peers; (3) promoter holding fell from ~25% (2001) to ~8.6% (2008) and much of it was pledged; (4) 16 Dec 2008 board approved a $1.6 bn purchase of promoter-family Maytas Properties/Infra (unrelated real estate) -- reversed in 12 hours after investor revolt; (5) World Bank debarred Satyam in Dec 2008; (6) independent directors resigned in late Dec 2008. Auditor PwC signed off for years (later penalised by SEBI/US PCAOB). Who spotted it: institutional investors who revolted against Maytas; some analysts flagged the unexplained cash yield. Lesson: test that cash earns market interest (interest income / average cash), compare promoter holding trend and pledges, and treat any related-party acquisition proposal by a cash-rich company as a disqualifier.

**Lesson:** Fake cash shows up as low other income; related-party deals by cash-rich firms are a disqualifier
**Spotted early by:** institutional investors (Maytas revolt), forensic-minded analysts
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:disqualifiers`, illustrates -> `insight:forensic-redflag-checklist`, illustrates -> `insight:auditor-exit-signal`
**Sources:** <https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyam_scandal> ; <https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/scandal-at-satyam-truth-lies-and-corporate-governance/> ; <https://www.business-standard.com/article/technology/satyam-loses-rs-10k-cr-in-m-cap-109010700071_1.html> ; <https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/101030/satyam-stock-crashes/>

`person:group-srei-kanoria` · flag: **severe** · confidence: verified · tickers: SREINFRA

Flag: SEVERE. Kolkata infrastructure/equipment financier: Srei Infrastructure Finance (SIFL, listed) and Srei Equipment Finance (SEFL). After the IL&FS shock (2018) and COVID, Srei sought a one-shot debt restructuring via a scheme of arrangement (2020-21) that lenders rejected. RBI superseded both boards (4-Oct-2021) citing governance concerns and payment defaults -- one of the first NBFCs sent to IBC by RBI; an RBI special audit had flagged related-party transactions and under-provisioning. A lender-commissioned KPMG forensic audit flagged transactions; Hemant Kanoria challenged its methodology (NCLT Kolkata dismissed his application); a separate BDO transaction audit was commissioned by the administrator to identify avoidance transactions. PNB reported an alleged Rs 2,434 cr loan fraud by the former promoters to RBI (2022); the Kanorias deny wrongdoing and call the matter sub judice; they also made a late offer to take Srei out of insolvency (2023), which was not accepted. NCLT Kolkata approved National ARC (NARCL)'s plan (CoC vote 89.2%), and NARCL took control; existing equity effectively wiped out. Early signals: high exposure to promoter-linked/infra SPVs, evergreening via group entities, auditor emphasis matters, and wholesale funding dependence. Lesson: in lenders, related-party exposure and regulatory special audits are the first reliable signal; the equity goes to near zero when the regulator supersedes the board.

- **regulator findings:** RBI supersession Oct-2021; RBI special audit RPT flags
- **allegations:** PNB fraud report Rs 2,434 cr (denied)

**Date:** 2026-11-21 · **Purpose:** the third test of `deep_dive_protocol.md`, and the first on a **US filer**. The aim is to adapt the protocol to SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, DEF 14A, Form 4, 13F, 13G). Run #1 (VMM) was an Indian retailer; run #2 (Cummins India) was an Indian manufacturer/MNC subsidiary.
**This is test material (lesson L9). There is no buy/sell/watchlist verdict and none should be read in.** It is research, not investment advice.
**Open paper call on this stock:** `thesis:paper-call:US-FIVE:fy2026-comps-11pct-plus` (P = 0.58 that FY2026 comps ≥ +11.0%). This file does **not** change that call. Relevant facts are noted in §9.

Every number carries a source tag. Every estimate shows its method.
- `[10K25]` = Form 10-K for FY2025 (year ended 31-Jan-2026), filed 19-Mar-2026, acc. 0001177609-26-000010 · `[10K24]` = 10-K FY2024, filed 20-Mar-2025
- `[PR-Qn FYyy]` = earnings press release, the Ex-99.1 of an Item 2.02 8-K. Q1 FY25 = 4-Jun-2025, Q2 FY25 = 27-Aug-2025, Q3 FY25 = 3-Dec-2025, Q4 FY25 = 18-Mar-2026, Q1 FY26 = 3-Jun-2026, Q2 FY26 = 2-Sep-2026 · `[PR-HOL25]` = holiday sales 8-K, 12-Jan-2026
- `[8K-date]` = other 8-Ks: officer changes (Item 5.02), the ABL amendment (Item 1.01, 14-Oct-2026), the cyber incident (Item 8.01, 22-Jul-2026)
- `[CC-Q2FY26]` = Q2 FY26 call, 2-Sep-2026. Taken from an automated transcript (webull) plus the Nasdaq call-highlights summary. **Single-source; names are garbled in places.**
- `[F4]` = Form 4s parsed by `tools/sec_fetch.py insider FIVE --limit 80` · `[13F]` = `sec_fetch.py holdings13f` · `[13G]` = Schedule 13G/A primary_doc.xml
- `[XBRL]` = `sec_fetch.py facts` (companyfacts) for FIVE, OLLI, DG and DLTR
- `[WEB]` = secondary web summary, single-source unless stated · `[EST]` = my estimate, with the method shown in the same row
- Fiscal years: FY2025 = 2-Feb-2025 to 31-Jan-2026. FY2026 = 1-Feb-2026 to 30-Jan-2027.

Context only: FY25 close $191.64 `[10K25]`. Insider sales in Sep-2026 were at $241–255 `[F4]`. BlackRock's 13F implies ~$220 at 30-Sep-2026 [EST: $1,206.6M ÷ 5.495M shares]. No valuation work was done, by design.
